wiki_only_topics.topic: Distinction between achievement and coat of arms
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: Sometimes the term " coat of arms " is used to refer to the full achievement, but this usage is incorrect in the strict sense of heraldic terminology, as a coat of arms refers to a garment with the escutcheon or armorial achievement embroidered on it.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Modern funerary usage of hatchment versus non-funereal achievement
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: In modern English, however, the term "hatchment" has come to be used almost exclusively to denote a funerary hatchment, while the word "achievement", now archaic in that sense, is used in place of "hatchment" in non-funereal contexts.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Historical statute of the Order of the Garter under Henry VIII
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: An example of the historic use of "hatchment" in a non-funerary context to denote what is now termed "achievement" appears in the statute of the Order of the Garter laid down by King Henry VIII (r. 1509–1547) concerning the regulation of Garter stall plates: It is agreed that every knyght within the yere of his stallation shall cause to be made a scauchon of his armes and hachementis in a plate of metall suche as shall please him and that it shall be surely sett upon the back of his stall.
